title: Foreigners and the People of God
lead: How the Bible treats outsiders: the resident foreigner (ger) protected by Israel's law, foreigners who joined Israel like Rahab and Ruth, laws that kept some nations at a distance, the prophets' vision of the nations coming to God, and the New Testament welcome of Gentiles into the church.

sections.b: God's promise to Abraham includes "all the clans of the earth" (Genesis 12:3), and "a mixed crowd" left Egypt with Israel (Exodus 12:38); a foreigner could keep the Passover once circumcised (Exodus 12:48–49). The Law protects the resident foreigner (ger): "love the foreigner, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 10:19). Some nations were kept at a distance (Deuteronomy 23:3–8), and after the exile Ezra led a covenant to send away foreign wives and their children (Ezra 9–10), while Nehemiah made men swear to stop such marriages (Nehemiah 13:23–27). Isaiah promises that foreigners who hold fast to the covenant will be welcome in God's house (Isaiah 56:3–7). In Acts, Peter learns that God accepts Gentiles (Acts 10), and Paul writes that they are "no longer strangers and aliens" (Ephesians 2:19).

sections.b:
The Bible both forbids and honors marriage across peoples. The patriarchs send for wives from their own kin rather than from the Canaanites (Genesis 24:3; Genesis 28:1). Joseph marries an Egyptian priest's daughter (Genesis 41:45), Moses a Midianite and a Cushite (Exodus 2:21; Numbers 12:1), and when Miriam objects to the Cushite wife, God sides with Moses. Samson insists on a Philistine wife against his parents' wishes (Judges 14:3), and Esther, a Jewish woman, becomes the Persian king's queen (Esther 2:17). The law forbids marriage with the seven nations of Canaan, and the reason it gives is religious: "they will turn your sons away from following me" (Deuteronomy 7:4). It also allows a man to marry a woman taken in war (Deuteronomy 21:10–14). Shechem's offer to intermarry with Jacob's family ends in a massacre (Genesis 34:9), and Phinehas kills an Israelite and the Midianite woman he brought into the camp (Numbers 25:6–8).

Judges and Kings tell how mixed marriages led to the worship of other gods (Judges 3:6; 1 Kings 11:1–4; 1 Kings 16:31). After the exile, Ezra leads a covenant to send away foreign wives and their children (Ezra 9–10); the Hebrew never says plainly that it was carried out. Nehemiah rebukes men who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab and makes them swear not to give or take daughters in marriage again (Nehemiah 13:23–27), and Malachi calls marriage to "the daughter of a foreign god" unfaithfulness (Malachi 2:11). Against this, Isaiah tells the foreigner who joins the LORD not to say he will be separated from God's people (Isaiah 56:3–7), and Ruth, Rahab and Tamar, all outsiders, stand in the line of David (Ruth 4:13–17; Matthew 1:3–5). In the New Testament, Paul tells believers not to leave an unbelieving spouse who wants to stay (1 Corinthians 7:12–14). Shaye Cohen and Christine Hayes trace how later Judaism turned these texts into rules on descent and conversion.
